questions.question: How do you sort in Ruby and what's the time complexity?
questions.title: Basic Sorting in Ruby
questions.direct_answer: Ruby's sort (and sort_by) uses a fast built-in (quicksort/merge, O(n log n) average). You call arr.sort (natural order) or arr.sort { |a, b| a <=> b } (custom), and sort_by { |x| x.len } for sorting by a key (stable and preferred for complex keys). For small or learning cases you may write bubble/insertion/selection sort by hand (all O(n^2)) to show you understand them, but in real code you use the built-in sort — it's O(n log n), tested, and faster than a hand-written one. Know the O(n^2) ones for interviews; use sort_by in code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Ruby's sort is O(n log n) built-in, sort_by for a key, and can name the O(n^2) sorts (bubble/insertion/selection).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing a hand-rolled O(n^2) sort in real code (use the built-in sort_by), or confusing sort (a<=>b) with sort_by (key).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Ruby's sort/sort_by is O(n log n) built-in; sort_by { |x| key } for a key. O(n^2) sorts (bubble/insertion/selection) for interviews; use sort_by in code.

sections.content: Ruby's sort, and sort_by, uses a fast built-in — quicksort or mergesort, O(n log n) average. You call arr.sort for the natural order or arr.sort with a b a spaceship b for a custom comparator, and sort_by with x x dot len for sorting by a key, which is stable and preferred for complex keys. For small or learning cases you may write bubble, insertion, or selection sort by hand — all O(n^2) — to show you understand them, but in real code you use the built-in sort because it's O(n log n), tested, and faster than a hand-written one. Know the O(n^2) ones for interviews; use sort_by in code.

sections.title: Sorting in Ruby
sections.content:
```ruby
# Built-in sort (O(n log n))
[3, 1, 2].sort                         # [1, 2, 3]
[3, 1, 2].sort { |a, b| b <=> a }      # [3, 2, 1] (descending)

# sort_by a key (preferred for complex keys, stable)
words = %w[apple fig kiwi]
words.sort_by(&:length)               # ['fig', 'kiwi', 'apple']
people.sort_by { |p| [p.age, p.name] }  # by age then name

# Hand-rolled bubble sort (O(n^2)) — for learning/interviews
def bubble(arr)
  n = arr.length
  loop do
    swapped = false
    (1...n).each do |i|
      if arr[i - 1] > arr[i]
        arr[i - 1], arr[i] = arr[i], arr[i - 1]
        swapped = true
      end
    end
    break unless swapped
  end
  arr
end
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Writing a hand-rolled O(n^2) sort in real code (use the built-in sort_by).
Confusing sort (a<=>b comparator) with sort_by (a key function).
Not knowing the O(n^2) sorts (bubble/insertion/selection) for interviews.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Ruby's sort/sort_by is a fast built-in (quicksort/merge), O(n log n) average.
Use sort_by { |x| key } for sorting by a key (stable; preferred for complex keys).
sort uses a comparator (a <=> b); sort_by uses a key function (x.len).
Bubble, insertion, selection are O(n^2) — know them for interviews, not real code.
In real code, use the built-in sort_by — tested and faster than hand-rolled.
